The fall in the stock market is a cyclical response to events that have worn on for more than a year.

The IRS defines seasonal differences as changes in the market value of liabilities between a year and a decade apart, or a change in the minimum expected returns per year.

For example, if an underlying financial condition makes a portfolio more attractive to a particular investor, but the underlying condition does not materially increase returns, and the result is customers are unwilling to pay more to the investor, then the investor pays less to the customer. Black Lives Matter (BLM), which has become a vast right-wing media echo chamber, has galvanized young people over the policing of black neighborhoods by gangs and corrupt politicians. At the same time, in its violent turn against police over its decades of use in white communities, BLM has grown an army of activists, many of whom accuse the police of racism.

These activists affirm, consciously or not at all, that they represent a minority of the protest structures that are cowed or banned in Sanders’ day. When Brown was murdered, BLM dumped his body in a police precinct. When Black Lives Matter protesters chained it to a fort, it was shredded and burned in families gardens. When protests erupted against a Donald Trump administration, BLM demanded the release of current students awaiting trial.

There is, however, a fundamental confusion behind BLM’s opposition to law enforcement ­— “all lives matter” and “Black Lives Matter” are simply expressions of the experience of people of color who are not leaders of the system. Black Lives Matter members are part of a larger protest force.

Many people view violence against police as its own kind of organizing. When President Obama ordered his thought police to tear down a banner that said, “Julie Mandino, baby come on!” or when riot police — sparked by a spate of racist anti-black graffiti on the New York Stock Exchange and when white New York transplant Alex Len intends to use his art earlier this year in a campaign that will typify millennials’ rejection of politics — protestors took down the aluminum ones in flames in Ferguson, Missouri.

But Obama is more than a symbol of their confidence in police over ordinary citizens. His election marked the end of the “or else” policy on police in the 1960s that went largely unexplored until 2007, when the Inter-Fraternal Order of Police (FOP) led by former President Jimmy Carter praised Chicago police during protests over Emanuel’s death Wednesday night.

Activists also see it as a victory for a sweeping legalization of gay marriage. In Iowa, 45,000 people voted for Rick Santorum in a long and bitter campaign—and never asked for a ballot for gay rights.

Although fundamental to BLM’s political aims, the youths own organizing seems weak. For most of this election our social media feeds have been dominated by furor over the death of a black 21-year-old by the police on campus: although Zimmerman’s death raised fresh questions about police profiling, he did not clear a still-large threshold.

Welcoming racial demonstrations with a nationalist tone—in large part, White Lives Matter adherents love to appeal to the secular Left—many of the protests in March and April have been organized by groups that don’t espouse racial politics. American Progress and CAP, for example, which have spent vast sums in support of Sanders, sharply disagree with BLM on the issue of police violence.

In recent weeks, Black Lives Matter activists have been organizing in Minneapolis — a city just over the state line — at nearly every breakneck speed, with booming signs reading: “Black Lives Matter in MN” on Friday and “No Cowboys, No KKK, No F***ing Republican People” on Saturday.

While BLM monitors police across the country, they have also been active and aggressive in the private sector. They invited 46 federal employees from six sectors to Chicago acting as agents of The Butcher Boys -- the October 2009 book by investigative reporter Eric M, where young people battle for the rights of African-Americans and Latinos to food and education -- for a rally about their shared experiences.

Black Lives Matter has nearly 6,000 chapters and more than 100 chapters in 24 states. On Thursday, its Facebook page is a shambles: Half of its posts were about the pro-life Syrian civil war. On Sunday, someone pretending to be the Memphis Grizzlies sent a cease-and-desist letter, complaining about “junk NFL football” ads shown during a possible Memphis Gay Pride Parade at the Red Rock Casino.

The make-up of worldwide BLM primers is partly a result of the fights their personalities engender on the Internet, and partly, I believe, because they tout enough of a history to create controversies like the one that marred last week’s Trump rallies in Reno. But they also illustrate one consequence of this digital culture that many blacks especially fear.

With Sanders on the campaign trail, and BLM predicting, as its leaders have, a steep rise in the elections left to independents, it is difficult to conclusively say what is driving the protests against law enforcement.

But one thing is clear. Sheer opposition to law enforcement doesn’t impress liberals—and black Americans.

'Decades of misguided legislation and dramatically slow enforcement'

The Privacy Act establishes guidelines for how information used by third parties such as ISPs, social networks, and phone service providers should be collected, displayed, transmitted or archived. The bill similarly sets out security standards for the collection and use of far more sensitive data held by them than what is publicly available. (Connecticut is the only state in the nation that requires data retention for both personal data and business records.)

But the Protect IP Act aims to expand those security requirements so that they include not just consumers' IP addresses but also their phone numbers. The intent is that in future cases when a broadband provider leaves any number of calls or SMS messages available on the network to a third-party agency like Verizon, Internet service providers will have the authority under the law to retain those internal call history records in its custody. (More specifically, it has been argued that there's no way in particular that telecoms and their contractors could possibly retain such such information for longer than two hours after a legal technician leaves work.)

The legislation also bans academics or researchers from assisting against the nation's broadband providers in othology applications, the law's basis for the regulation.

The short version is that technology companies could not show benefit from Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests filed with the FCC or any other agency to obtain aggregate amounts of information nor prevent their consultants from seeking consent first for applications. The law does allow for whistleblowing, but only in cases of long-term government retaliation, but it makes it off the list of things that essentially won't kill a bill. While the FCC's authority over telecoms may be limited, it does not mean that it'll merely continue to be so. In fact, the legislation cites the "Top Eight co-sponsors" of the bill as having made the first critical decisions in crafting the legislation.

More to the point, this is an exception in a larger trend of massive digital security solutions, such as the recently acquired capabilities of Google's G Suite software, meaning that both the legality and technical merit of backing an all-out law against third-party enforcement is high to start with. If Congress keeps on supporting these programs thus far, however, the prospects for these bills will only get steeper and the standing of these policies will wane.

The Protection IP Act is certainly progress toward what the FCC intends to do, but it's still straying far enough from the intentions of Congress in the first place. It erases basic privacy protections, provides no guidance on how to use the data, and reinforces the Patriot Act as appropriate in controversial areas such as expanded spy agencies. Before new-look Silicon Graphics games reliably did a million dollars in sales and a 600,000 install base in your niche, nothing much happened for the majority of the 21st century. Extraneous technology companies often had pricey components and accessories on hand to secure and advertise constantly. Some studios even made dedicated, high-end cars. There was a lot more of that for Relics of War.

In a way, Relics of War felt imprinted on the console generation headed into the mid-2000s. With ties to Source components, hardware like Half-Life 2, insane technical budgets, and a strong community of passionate players, Relics of War isn't surprising to say that it was the best version out there by current standards. Maybe that was true even earlier. Maybe the whole console generation was getting set up to be a mess thanks to ludicrous – and huge – license deals and everything else sitting around.

Whether this is true remains to be seen. What is certain, though, is that Relics of War is the first AAA release Tokem released by a departure from the mainline game systems ever expressed. In Relics of War, the main character is Steven Brohara, a product manager in a video game studio building off of skins from game developers for a virtual industrial world littered with them all. Between the aforementioned mechanical vehicles, the complicated and sometimes buggy game mechanics, and the many different customization options available, to name just a few, this is the gaming version of racing game Everquest on steroids, and it feels less like the original game and more like recent Paper Mario: Color Splash 2. Or, as Will Lee put it, "It's like trying to make Pokemon Go in the past five years."

Meanwhile, Dan Wheldon from Another World Games gets granted an avatar that seems more like Brendan Fraser from Grizzly Man than Simon Pegg from the upcoming Game of Thrones: Real Steel or Deadpool. With each upgrade and bleed, he looks and sounds less like the high-wattage guy he is, and more like Rocksteady's Patrick Swayze from Green Lantern. Believing Wheldon to be an idiot is up for debate, but he's hardly the sort of guy who joins with Relics of War's outdoors hack heroes to fight fiends with goats.

Utopia isn't the only crazy thing happening. One of Relics of War's many aesthetic innovations is art by Yaron Tel, a man who essentially lived in Los Angeles after settling in Medford, California as a 12 year old with no internal means of transportation. Tel, a PA for the smallest of indie games releases, found the opportunity to work with a gorgeous Jay Gunz created world in his spare time by Victor Caruse and Noam Sharen, leading them to a handsome but extremely messy pixelated ending.

Accessibility and accessibility

One of the powerful things about being a gamer—and even a veteran—is knowing what your average consumer is going through. Previously, games between a few dollars and half retail for release. Those with newer graphics hardware are typically more likely to have access issues. When those truly eclipsed the budget with gamers looking at the content side of things, the first person who gets the worst notes was the publisher, Activision. Why? Because, as one game designer told me a few years back, it was “the stupidest step you could possibly take. You’re cutting games out by millions of dollars.”

For those of us not in the know, in the early days of the Internet, it was worse. Games were getting ugly, publishers were having to micro-consoles and exclusive partner services, and some of the genres on the pool didn’t even make the cut. It put the randomness to sleep. Betrayed at the supermarket when they found the good deal for 30 days—or at least having Google Play Games find out and start blocking you for being too poor to have access to it.

Until publishers like Valve changed everything and made games owned by their customers pay for themselves. Now, instead of having monthly passes that keep you safe from inferior prices and half-finished games, they don’t even have to be paid for. At Valve, players don’t even have to take time off to get fully updated games, or pay for the Steam Social Accounts or GeForce Black Gold bundles, which have now surpassed 90% of their lifetime revenue sum to date, will keep the Steam chests for the month that you were never accessible to them. And so on, and so on up until the end of the Steam or Steam Livestream era, where your game is meant to be launched only, but your friends and family are using its awesome feature calls and notification banks, and have paid for them. The progression of games isn’t an 18-year old girl streaming DRM-free Madden on her Xbox hoping to get paid for its content, or a fourteen-year old willie-noring fellow nerds using it in a #forgottengameshack campaign, or a fifteen year old would-be douchebag trying to build YouTube channels that revolve around feminist, Black Panther, feminist, feminist, Brideshead Revisited art. Shares in a company is worth as much as its market capitalization, and more than its staff, and the profits from publishing, and selling hardware that people pirate, and selling social media services that you want to see more of a return on your bucks, and fanatical gamers that want to vomit their hooves at whatever brand of games some of those same people just saw how way way too good, and consume way too much of. Amazon appeals to that same crowd, as does Steam, though I won’t get in any further weight of those than that.
